name: Monthly OPM Hours and Activity Driver surveys
change: Pre-fill the Hours survey with last month's hours (no reply means confirm) and replace driver surveys with existing standard reports.
reason: The mail shows both parts of the change were already in place: the Hours survey already carried a 'Last Month' column, managers with unchanged hours could already just send an email, and every driver survey since April already invited groups to send a standard report instead, so the claimed 20 minutes saved per manager is not supported.
research: Look for mail showing what still takes managers' time after these options existed and after the September 2000 move to Access (for example, how many groups actually switched to sending reports, or complaints about the Access survey), and build the proposal on that remaining gap.

name: Monthly OPM hours and activity driver surveys
change: Pre-fill the OPM hours survey from last month, make the commercial-team split required, and take driver counts from standard reports instead of the spreadsheet.
reason: Two of the three changes already exist in the mail (FTE and commercial-team rollover, a prior-month hours report, and the standing offer to accept standard reports instead of the driver survey), and the 1,630 minutes a month rests on a padded headcount (the 50 on 2080.eml include cc'd directors and the OPM staff), a skipped-month frequency, and guessed per-person and chase figures.
research: Find mail showing how many managers actually fill in the hours survey each month, how long it takes them, how many RCs took up the report option and why the others did not, and how often the OPM team has to chase missing commercial-team splits; a proposal limited to the required-split check, or to pre-filling the hours themselves, might hold up on that evidence.

name: Monthly OPM hours and activity-driver surveys
change: Pre-fill each manager's hours survey from ATEs headcount and last month's split, and replace driver surveys with standard system reports, so managers only confirm changes.
reason: The mail shows most of the change was already in place (the Access hours survey rolled over FTEs and commercial teams and printed prior-month hours by activity, unchanged months needed only an email, and every driver survey already offered a standard report instead), so the minutes saved are not supported; two critics have already rejected the same work for this reason.
research: Find mail showing what still costs managers time in the Access survey after rollover existed, how many RCs actually switched to sending reports and why others did not, and how often OPM chases missing surveys; a proposal aimed only at that remaining gap (for example an automatic missing-survey list from ATEs) might hold up.

name: Monthly OPM activity-driver and hours surveys
change: Pull activity-driver counts from system reports and pre-fill the hours survey with last month's figures so managers only confirm changes
reason: The mail shows the OPM team had already built most of this: from September 2000 the hours survey ran in an Access tool that carries over commercial teams and headcount and shows last month's hours, and the activity-driver survey does not appear after August 2000, so the claimed 1,064 minutes a month are mostly not there to save.
research: Look for activity-driver survey requests after August 2000 and for time spent on the Access hours survey after it carried data over (from March 2001 on); only the gap between showing last month's hours in a report and pre-filling them could still be saved, and that needs its own evidence.

name: Monthly OPM hours and activity driver surveys
change: Pre-fill the OPM hours survey with last month's hours and Org Database/ATEs positions, take driver quantities from standard reports, and treat non-responders as carry-forward.
reason: Most of the change already exists in the mail (since the September 2000 Access survey, FTEs and commercial teams roll over and a prior-month hours report is built in; unchanged-hours managers could already just email; every driver survey already offered to accept a standard report), so the 'today' describes a retired spreadsheet process and the 915 minutes a month saved is unsupported; this is also the third proposal for the same work, already rejected twice in decisions.md.
research: Find mail from after the Access rollout showing what still costs managers time, such as how long the survey takes, how many RCs actually switched to sending reports and why others did not, or how often OPM must chase missing surveys, and limit the proposal to that remaining gap.

name: Strangers Gas write-off approval memos

reason: The memos are a one-time cleanup of old 1999-2000 flows sent in a burst from Dec 2000 to Jan 2001, not steady monthly work. Only about 5 of the roughly 20 memos are small enough for the threshold, so the claim that most are small and the rate of 8 small items a month are both wrong.
research: Look for Strangers Gas write-off memos about current-month flow after January 2001, or in other mailboxes, that show small items keep coming at a steady rate.

name: Monthly OPM hours and activity-driver surveys
change: Pre-fill the hours survey from last month and ATEs headcount, take driver counts from existing reports, and automate reminders.
reason: The proposal describes the June 2000 process as today's, but the mail shows it was replaced: from October 2000 the hours survey ran in an Access tool that rolls over commercial teams and FTE headcount and reports last month's hours (1415, 1436, 2015, 2080), every driver survey already offered a standard report instead (856 to 1244), and no driver survey appears after the July 2000 one (1319), so the 1,655 minutes a month are mostly not there to save; four critics have already rejected this same work for this reason.
research: Find mail from 2001 on showing what still costs managers time in the Access hours survey once rollover worked (complaints, help calls, late returns), how many groups actually switched to sending reports, and any driver-survey requests after August 2000; only a proposal aimed at that remaining gap, such as pre-filling the hours themselves or an automatic list of missing surveys from ATEs, could hold up.

name: Calpine daily gas nomination handling
change: Replace Calpine's emailed Word nomination, phone call and confirmation email with a structured nomination that rolls forward and needs a reply only when it changes.
reason: The mail shows only that Calpine emails a Word nomination on weekdays; the phone call on every day, the HPL confirmation loop, the re-keying and the daily-including-weekends rate are not supported, and the estimate counts Calpine's own time, so the 13 minutes a day is not realistic.
research: Look in the schedulers' mailboxes (Robert Lloyd, Aimee Lannou, Juliann Kemp) for what HPL does with the Calpine nomination: replies or confirmations sent to Calpine, keying errors or corrections, or revised nominations that caused rework. Evidence like that could support a smaller weekday-only saving for the Enron scheduler.

research: Find scheduler replies to Ricky Archer's nominations, and nomination contents or comparisons that show how often Calpine's daily volumes actually repeat; also whether HPL had an electronic nomination entry Calpine could use.

research: Look for ongoing expired-deal or no-deal requests after January 2001 (Lannou, Young, Olsen, McCoy, Poorman and others) to show a steady monthly rate, and for traders extending deals unchanged, to show how many could safely roll forward; a proposal limited to batching the existing feedback-monitor list for one approval might hold up on that evidence.

name: Calpine daily gas nomination to HPL scheduler

research: Find short-term MDQ, extension or continuation requests in other TW marketers' or Contract Administration's mail (Dennis Lee, Michael Bodnar, TK Lohman, Paul Y'Barbo, Lindberg, McConnell) outside December 2001, and anything showing how long Contract Admin spends on a one- or two-day amendment.
